At Nepal’s border with China, flash floods devastated the town of Timure, leaving bodies scattered across the country’s worst-hit area. With many victims dismembered, decomposed and stripped of clothing, forensic teams are relying on DNA testing to identify the dead.

title: UN raises concern for women and girls amid mounting death toll in Nepal floods - Jurist.org
description: UN raises concern for women and girls amid mounting death toll in Nepal floods  Jurist.org
publisher.title: Jurist.org
full_article:
The United Nations stated Tuesday that Nepal’s catastrophic flash floods had killed more than 1,000 people, while thousands remain missing. The statement especially noted that women and girls face shortages of food, safe water, healthcare and protection in the wake of the disaster.

The UN provided an estimate of 4,247 people who remained unaccounted for as search-and-rescue operations continued. The disaster was triggered on August 26 by a glacier collapse and landslide near Nepal’s border with China, sending floodwater and debris through settlements and infrastructure along river corridors.

The disaster severely affected the mountainous districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading, destroying homes, roads, bridges, water systems and health facilities resulting in severe access constraints faced by humanitarian officials. The co ntinuing monsoon rains, unstable slopes and blocked waterways have hampered rescue operations and left several remote communities difficult to reach.

UN Women estimated that 43,000 women and girls required immediate humanitarian assistance. Christine Arab, the agency’s Regional Director for Asia and the Pacific, said women survivors were running out of food, losing access to safe water and confronting heightened protection risks. Nearly 160,000 women and girls in Rasuwa and Nuwakot had been directly or indirectly affected, according to an earlier UN Women assessment.

Arab warned that the floods had exacerbated pre-existing inequalities: women in affected communities already travelled long distances to collect water, and the destruction of roads, bridges and water systems had cut off supplies. Moreover, displacement and the absence of safe, separate sanitation facilities, lighting and privacy also increased exposure to gender-based violence, trafficking and exploitation. This also resulted in women-headed households facing particular pressure because male migration was common in the affected areas.

The World Health Organization also warned of possible secondary health emergencies. Flooding, overcrowding, displacement and stagnant water could increase the risk of dengue, scrub typhus and other communicable diseases. Additionally, UNICEF reported that at least 17,000 children had been affected and appealed for $17.2 million for emergency response and early recovery efforts.

title: NH Nepali community raises money for disaster relief in Nepal - New Hampshire Public Radio
description: NH Nepali community raises money for disaster relief in Nepal  New Hampshire Public Radio
publisher.title: New Hampshire Public Radio
full_article:
New Hampshire is home to around 3,500 people from Nepal or of Nepali heritage, according to local Nepali community leaders. Many of those people live in the Manchester area, and many of them have firsthand connections to people impacted by the devastating flooding and landslide that hit the country last week .

“We have one particular community member who lost his uncle [and] 35 relatives,” said Madhab Gurung, vice president of the NH Nepali Community group. He said many others also lost family members, while even more have lost homes back in Nepal amid the destruction.

The group has been raising money for disaster relief efforts. As of Thursday afternoon, it raised about $84,000 according to Gurung. He said that support has come from a wide array of Granite Staters, including Nepali people but also many other concerned locals.

Additionally, the group has hosted vigils to honor the victims, including one in Manchester and another in front of the statehouse in Concord.

As the hot sun beats down in Kathmandu, Santosh Swaminathan and his cousin Nathan Subramanian take a break from searching for their missing loved ones to stop at a temple and pray.

After they lost contact with Swaminathan’s sister and her husband following the devastating flood last week, they flew from India to Nepal. But as they wait for the army to rebuild roads and bridges into the areas where their loved ones were, they’re getting desperate.

Like other families of missing Australians, they’re now taking matters into their own hands. They’re hiring four-wheel drives and heading into the flood zones to search.

View image in fullscreen Nathan Subramanian, 45, left, and his cousin Santosh Swaminathan, 42, are in Nepal hoping to make contact with Swaminathan’s sister Chitra Venkatraman, 46, who was travelling with her husband. Photograph: Cait Kelly/The Guardian

Swaminathan’s sister Chitra Venkatraman, 46, and her husband, Venkatraman Balakrishnan, 52, were among 15 Australians travelling to Mount Kailash, on a spiritual trip with the Himalayan Glacier Adventures tour group. In total, more than 5,000 people have been reported missing in Nepal and a further 546 in the Tibet region of China after the flooding, which has killed more than 1,200 people. Thirty-six Australians remain unaccounted for.

“They are just fun-loving people,” Swaminathan, 42, says of the missing New South Wales couple. “My sister, she is so funny … They are a very loving family. We miss them very badly right now.”

‘How do I not crumble?’ Loved ones of Australians missing in Nepal-Tibet floods fear others are turning away Read more

On the weekend, the pair hired a 4WD in the capital, Kathmandu, and headed up the valley. The conditions are dangerous: roads collapse under cars, landslides are common and near-constant rain makes it hard to see. There are long delays, and when parts of the road slide away, travellers jump out of their cars to fill holes back in with rocks. Parts of the valley don’t have power, and there is no clean water or food.

But Subramanian, 45, says they had to try. They managed to get to Trishuli, a town roughly 40km from Kathmandu but still another 20km from where the Australians would have been in Syabru Besi.

“We took a car, food, everything,” Subramanian says. “The conditions are very bad. It’s been really bad – after Trishuli, there was no more road.

“It was a risk, a very high risk. But that is all we can do. As family members, we need to do whatever we can do.”

The day after their attempt, there was a huge mudslide on the road just down from Trishuli, leaving army personnel, aid workers and journalists stranded overnight.

Other families sent another search car up on Wednesday to look for the missing group, which is made up of Canadians, Americans, Singaporeans, British citizens and Australians. They are hoping they can get all the way to the area where the group was staying.

“We are just trying whatever we can,” Swaminathan says.

View image in fullscreen Chitra Venkatraman, 46, and her husband, Venkatraman Balakrishnan, 52, were among 15 other Australians travelling to Mount Kailash, on a spiritual trip with the Himalayan Glacier Adventures tour group. Photograph: supplied

There’s two pieces of information buoying the families from the group. First, the group was around a 45-minute drive from the area of the border with Tibet which was decimated by the wall of water and rock that ran down the valley. Second, the phones of other members of the group pinged last Wednesday – one as late as 2.30pm, hours after the flood hit.

In Kathmandu, the family have visited the Australian and Indian embassies. They’ve spoken to Nepali politicians. They’ve been handing over any leads to police, and visiting the hospitals as the injured and dead start to arrive from Rasuwa, where the worst of the flooding hit.

Swaminathan is in contact with the couple’s son, Akash Venkatraman, 22, who lives in Sydney with his younger brother. He says they’re being supported by family there.

Locator for Nepal flash floods

On Tuesday, the Australian ambassador to Nepal, Simon Ernst, warned families against heading into the flood zone.

“We do understand for those with missing loved ones what an incredibly difficult time this must be,” he said. “Please do be assured we are working around the clock … to locate loved ones.

“And a reminder, please, avoid travel to the impacted area. We remain in the monsoon season; the risk of further flooding is very real and furthermore, access to flood-damaged areas is very difficult, if not impossible.”

A lack of technology available to the Nepali army has hampered the search efforts.

On Thursday, the Australian government announced it was deploying a team of specialist drone operators to contribute to the search efforts. But families are questioning why Nepal didn’t ask for technical help sooner.

Subramanian says he knows the army is doing its best and trusts their capabilities, but acknowledges the technology they have access to is limited.

View image in fullscreen The day after the cousins’ attempt, there was a huge mudslide on the road just down from Trishuli, leaving army personnel, aid workers and journalists stranded overnight. Photograph: YONHAP/AFP/Getty Images

“Ideally on the first day, they should have actually taken support from other governments,” he says. “Things could have been different.”

In the heat and chaos of Kathmandu, the pair are trying everything they can. Running on anxiety and adrenaline, they are determined to bring their family members home.

“Today we are in a situation where we don’t know what to do tomorrow,” Subramanian says.

“We don’t know what’s next. We are just trying to turn over every stone that we can as civilians. We believe they are still alive, and now we are begging for a miracle.”

full_article:
With roads and bridges severed, helicopters became the main rescue lifeline

Nepal’s first female helicopter Captain Priya Adhikari, flew around 100 rescue missions. She described navigating a narrow valley with up to 20 helicopters at once while evacuating survivors



Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.



Trishuli Bazaar: With roads and bridges severed across Rasuwa and Nuwakot after the Aug 26 Bhote Koshi-Trishuli flood, helicopters became the main rescue lifeline, airlifting more than 4,000 people in hundreds of sorties through a narrow gorge in what officials described as possibly Nepal's biggest such operation.Pilots said the missions were tougher than Everest-season flying, with wrong coordinates, landing spots buried under mud, crowded skies, drones and false rescue alerts complicating operations.Talking to TOI at Maithili Barracks, where choppers were taking off and landing in Trishuli Bazaar, Captain Bimal Sharma of Simrik Air said Everest flights, despite the altitude, were more predictable. "Even during the climbing season on Everest, it's still busy, but there's a clear goal of where to go and what to do." Here, he said, coordinates often did not match and pilots sometimes reached places where the landing ground itself had vanished. "We have to search around. In some places where we were asked to land, there was no place to do that."At times, over a dozen helicopters operated simultaneously between Trishuli and the Tibet border. There was no separate airport in the flood-hit area, leaving pilots to work in effectively uncontrolled airspace once inside the gorge.Pilots devised their own rules - keeping left in valleys, announcing positions and maintaining altitude gaps.Captain Maniraj Lama of Kailash Helicopter said the missions changed by the day. Initially, choppers carried doctors and rescuers in and survivors out. They then shifted to food and relief drops; later, as bodies began decomposing at inaccessible sites, crews started lifting some by longline beneath the helicopter.Drones added another hazard. Civil aviation authority of Nepal joint spokesperson Gyanendra Bhul said pilots relied on visual separation and direct communication. "Right now, the biggest challenge for helicopters there is from those drones," he said.False alerts became a recurring drain on flying time. Old and unverified videos kept circulating for days, repeatedly sending helicopters and drones towards places where nobody was found. After one claim that people were stranded in forests around Ghattekhola, national emergency operations centre chief Phanindra Prasad Poudel said, "We even had a helicopter hold the area for 19 minutes. We also monitored it with drones. But nothing was found there."

KATHMANDU, Nepal (AP) — Some survivors sheltering in relief camps after deadly floods in Nepal struggled Thursday to obtain essential medicines and cash, even as authorities provided food and other basic supplies to thousands of displaced people.

The shortages are adding to the hardships of those living in temporary shelters after having lost homes and belongings.

Suresh Kumar Karanjit, who has been staying at a relief center in Devighat, a town in one of the worst-affected areas in Nuwakot district, lost his younger brother in the floods last week. He said the camp did not have the exact medicine prescribed for his heart condition.

Karanjit only managed to get the cash he needed to buy his regular medicine after selling a carton of noodles he received as relief for 400 rupees ($2.60). “We have been living here for a week. The relief materials are being provided, which is good. But there is a lack of medicine,” he said.

The Aug. 26 floods that were likely caused by a glacier collapse devastated towns and valleys in Nepal, destroying homes, roads, bridges and other critical infrastructure. title: ‘They’ll be finding bodies next year’: a renowned forensic scientist on Nepal’s ‘extreme challenges’ - The Guardian

full_article:
The bodies of some of those killed in the Nepal-Tibet flood disaster may never be found, and some of those that are may never be identified, a world-renowned forensic scientist says.

Prof Richard Bassed, the head of forensic medicine at Melbourne’s Monash University, spent three months in Thailand after the 2004 Boxing Day tsunami and also helped to identify victims of Victoria’s catastrophic Black Saturday bushfires in 2009.

Now he has watched as authorities in Nepal and Tibet struggle to find and identify the dead amid the agonies of the living after last week’s devastating flash flood. More than 1,250 people have been confirmed dead, with more than 5,000 missing.

Prakrit has already lost her father. As Nepal’s morgues fill, she hopes her DNA can be used to find her mother Read more

The difficult terrain, and inadequate communications and resources, would all hamper efforts, Bassed says.

“They could be washed anywhere, buried under mud. I imagine there’s a number they’ll never find. I imagine they’ll be finding bodies next year.”

Authorities are still finding bodies from the 2011 Japanese tsunami, he says.

The bodies from the 2004 tsunami were relatively easy to recover, but it still took a year to identify 5,000 people, he says.

“And there were still some we couldn’t identify.”

Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email

Asked how he copes with the horror of death on such a scale, he says he has “never found it long-term traumatising”.

“Occasionally you’ll see something that’ll hit close to home. For me, it’s kids,” he says.

“And the randomness. The randomness of a tsunami, the randomness of this massive flood. That gets to you.

“But mostly you have your clinical face on, you do the best you can and know you’re doing it to help people.”

Authorities will use rapidly improving DNA techniques to try to identify the victims. This week Nepali police urged relatives of missing tourists to provide “a fresh blood sample for DNA profiling and two passport-sized photographs” to the pathology laboratory at the police hospital in Kathmandu.

But authorities in Nepal and Tibet face “extreme challenges”, Bassed says.

They include the danger of more mudslides, the complexity of co-ordinating across international borders and the likelihood of local mortuaries and other infrastructure being overwhelmed by the number of bodies.

The mix of nations and religions also brings issues of different cultural beliefs around how and whether people should be buried.

The International Committee of the Red Cross and other international bodies have published Management of dead bodies after disasters: A field manual for First Responders to help people deal with bodies in a “proper and dignified way”, including by taking down details that will later help experts identify the remains.

First responders – often locals who are not forensic experts – are trained to follow those guidelines, tagging bodies in the hope they will later be matched to a missing person.

They give each body a unique code (for example the name of the place, the name of the team and a number). They will also take photos of the body and any distinguishing features such as gold teeth, clothing and tattoos, including that code in the image.

View image in fullscreen ‘You have your clinical face on, you do the best you can’ … Prof Richard Bassed. Photograph: John Lloyd Fillingham / Victorian Institute of Forensic Medicine

Then they place the body in a body bag and organise its “orderly temporary storage”, again marked with the body code.

In Nepal, morgues are filling up and mass burials are taking place, as authorities collect DNA samples.

Bassed says most of the missing Australians would have dental records, which could help to identify them, but in Nepal many matches will be made using DNA or pictures, as fingerprints will often no longer be usable.

Work is under way to use AI and facial recognition technology to identify victims after disasters, but it’s controversial – Ukraine used Clearview AI software after the Russian invasion in 2022, just as the company was fined millions of dollars for collecting images of people in the UK and elsewhere without consent. Widespread use is also limited by access to the technology.

Bassed says researchers have also worked to devise an algorithm that could use passport or driver’s licence photos to identify someone.

“But it’s really complex, and it depends how they look, the trauma,” he says.

Another possibility is CT scanning, which can get a serial number from joint replacements, for example.

“But trying to get this technology to the places it’s needed in the middle of a disaster … you need running water, you need electricity … you could put CT scanners into helicopters, but all this costs an awful lot of money.”

title: AI-generated elephant rescue videos mislead online amid Nepal flooding - Yahoo
description: AI-generated elephant rescue videos mislead online amid Nepal flooding  Yahoo
publisher.title: Yahoo
full_article:
Days after flash floods along the Nepal-Tibet border in August 2026 killed hundreds of people, social media posts shared videos falsely claiming they showed elephants rescuing people from the floodwaters. While elephants have been reported helping people during floods in other instances, the videos contain visual inconsistencies indicative of AI-generated content.

"Not all superheroes are humans. They're sometimes animals too. Kudos to this elephant who helped a person cross safely. #FloodDisaster #Nepal," reads a Tagalog-language caption of a Facebook video shared on August 27.

The 20-second clip shows a man stranded in fast-moving floodwaters, with a person behind the camera yelling in Thai, "Hey! Hey! (Look at) the water!"

An elephant then suddenly appears, wades through the current and allows the man to climb onto its back before returning to land.

Similar videos also circulated in various social platforms in India, Pakistan, Australia and South Korea.

Another post shared on Threads on August 30, 2026 purportedly shows an elephant rescuing children.

"The floods in Nepal is really heartbreaking ㅠㅠ (...) I see many stories of elephants rescuing people ㅠㅠ" reads the post's Korean-language caption.

Comments such as "Thank you Lord, you directed the elephant to rescue the tiny angels" or "I pray all elephants will be treated as well as this young one treats people" suggest many believed the footage to be real.

While there were reports of elephants rescuing people from floods in Nepal in 2017, both videos shared recently were either uploaded online prior to the floods in August 2026 ( archived link).

The video also contains several inconsistencies commonly found in AI-generated media.
